rewrites.summary:
Federal criminal law governs visitor exposure in Enugu: same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, and the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act reaches those who arrange, attend or promote same-sex weddings or publicly promote LGBTQ+ organisations. Government travel guidance issued by a foreign ministry in August 2026 warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation, and notes that mobile networks can be suspended and curfews imposed with little notice.

Reporting on queer life under those laws documents threats and police raids alongside informal community organising, and public grief after the August 2024 murder of a well-known transgender figure in the federal capital. The murder and the raids it followed were reported in the capital, not in Enugu; no Enugu-specific statute, enforcement or protection is documented in the sources examined, so the state is assessed on the nationwide framework: criminalisation on the books, arbitrary policing, and violence that is rarely prosecuted.

The audited reporting of raids on queer gatherings and of the 2024 killing of an out transgender figure concerns the federal capital, not this state; no local divergence is documented in either direction, so the visitor stands under the national framework and its enforcement climate.

rewrites.summary:
Taraba sits under Nigeria's federal criminal law: same-sex conduct carries up to 14 years, and the Same-Sex Marriage Prohibition Act criminalises arranging, attending or promoting same-sex weddings and registering or publicly promoting gay groups. August 2026 foreign travel guidance warns LGBT+ travellers of arrest, violence, blackmail and intimidation anywhere in the country. The same reporting era records mass arrests and detentions of LGBTQ+ people as common, especially in northern states, and the August 2024 beating death of a widely followed transgender content creator in the federal capital, hours after a public post, with the murder left unsolved.

Some northern states add Sharia criminal provisions that can reach death-penalty outcomes; the audited sources do not place Taraba among the states applying them, and no Taraba-specific finding is documented either way. The visitor's profile here is the federal one: criminalisation on the statute book, arbitrary enforcement, and little protection against mob or individual violence.

No Banten-specific statute, ordinance, raid, protection or service is documented in anything examined. A visitor in Banten therefore stands under the national picture those sources sketch - no criminalisation of gender identity itself, rising official and vigilante hostility toward LGBT+ visibility, and weak accountability for mob violence - but this record asserts nothing beyond that shared, hedged base.

rewrites.summary:
The audited sources document Indonesia's national posture rather than Gorontalo: an October 2025 presidential decree lists "the promotion of LGBTQ+ culture" among non-military national-security threats alongside terrorism, radicalism and drug addiction; legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery plus judicial approval; a wave of vigilante mob attacks on trans women on 14-16 July 2026 - most severely more than fifteen people doused, stripped and beaten in Bogor, with footage circulated online - and researchers record markedly hardened anti-queer attitudes since 2016. Provincial moral enforcement is sharpest in Aceh, per the same feature.

Nothing in the audited material shows Gorontalo diverging in either direction: no documented local ordinance, raid wave, protection or service specific to the province. A visitor there is exposed to the national picture - identity not criminalised, visibility treated as a security threat, mob violence met with limited accountability.

No provincial-specific finding exists in the material; the visitor's exposure is the national climate, not any documented local rule.

rewrites.summary:
The audited sources for Sabah document Malaysia's federal and state-level framework rather than the province itself: same-sex conduct is criminalised under Section 377A with penalties up to 20 years and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and state-level syariah enactments penalise male cross-dressing; a 2022 human-rights report (retrieved as a fetch-time summary) documents state-backed discrimination - arrests, raids and prosecutions driven by state religious authorities - across the federation. The source files state expressly that they contain no unit-specific findings for Sabah.

Sabah is therefore assessed on the national framework alone: criminal provisions apply through the federal penal code as in the rest of Malaysia, religious-offence jurisdiction exists at state level, and no audited source supports treating this province as materially safer or harsher than the federal baseline.

The sources record no findings specific to this state; neither extra safety nor extra severity is documented, so the national framework applies without adjustment.
